title: Michigan Senate race: GOP's Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed face off in televised debate
text:
Photos by Robin Buckson-Pool/Getty Images OAN Staff Brooke Mallory
5:00 PM – Thursday, October 22, 2026
The final debate in the key swing-state race for Michigan’s U.S. Senate seat erupted into a fiery spectacle on Wednesday, as Republican nominee Mike Rogers and Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed delivered personal jabs and aggressive ideological contrasts.
Meeting on stage at the WXYZ Channel 7 studios in Southfield, Michigan, both contenders traded blows over allegations of foreign influence, the political influence of President Donald Trump, trade policy and gun violence.
The debate highlighted a deeply polarized campaign to succeed retiring Democrat Senator Gary Peters, offering voters sharply divergent visions on national security, domestic policy and personal integrity.
In the most explosive exchange of the evening, Rogers launched an attack accusing El-Sayed of being bought off by the Muslim Brotherhood and labeling him a national security risk.
El-Sayed, a former Detroit health director who would become the nation’s first Muslim U.S. senator if elected, denied his opponent’s claims while defending his alleged loyalty to the United States and constitutional commitment. Visibly angry, El-Sayed called Rogers’ allegations shameful and beneath the dignity of the race, emphasizing that he was born and raised in Michigan and remains proud of the U.S. Constitution that guarantees religious freedom for all Americans.
The candidates’ second major boiling point centered on their relationship with President Trump and his ongoing impact on the political landscape. Rogers, who secured Trump’s endorsement to win the Republican nomination, defended protectionist economic policies and hardline immigration enforcement while arguing that current economic missteps have driven up costs for Michigan families.
In contrast, El-Sayed linked Rogers directly to Trump’s roadmap, criticizing conservative foreign and economic policies for, in his own words, “driving inflation, spiking energy prices and creating global instability.”
Gun violence and Second Amendment rights was the topic of the third heated clash, exposing fundamental ideological divides on public safety. El-Sayed pushed for more extreme gun reform measures, emphasizing his background in public health to argue that gun violence should be treated as a urgent national health crisis requiring assault weapon restrictions.
Drawing on his background in law enforcement and federal intelligence, Rogers countered that strict gun control measures infringe on the constitutional rights of law-abiding citizens rather than addressing criminal behavior or underlying mental health challenges.
He emphasized that overly restrictive policies could prevent lawful gun owners from defending themselves or intervening against armed assailants in critical situations, referencing tragic mass shootings such as the recent attack on the elementary school in Bend, Oregon.
A fourth critical moment emerged as well during a debate on international trade and manufacturing jobs, a vital issue for Michigan’s industrial heartland. El-Sayed pressed Rogers on his long legislative record in the U.S. House of Representatives, accusing him of supporting trade deals that offshored American manufacturing jobs.
Rogers firmly rejected the allegations, pointing out that historical agreements like NAFTA were enacted long before his tenure in Congress and arguing that broad protective tariffs are essential to shield Michigan workers from foreign economic exploitation.
The fifth key clash saw both candidates questioning each other’s fitness to serve and accusing one another of taking money from special interests. While Rogers framed El-Sayed as an out-of-touch radical backed by fringe far-left groups, El-Sayed accused Rogers of being a secret corporate insider who sold out first responders and working-class voters.
With millions pouring into the competitive race, the televised showdown provided voters with an intense preview of the choices facing Michiganders heading into the election.

🟦 Abdul El-Sayed: 70%
